title: Just Keep Learning
author: Cultivated Soul
summary: A former classical-school teacher traces her path from an uneven, mostly self-directed education to four years in the University of Chicago's Basic Program in the Great Books. She moved from solitary reading and book clubs to Susan Wise Bauer's reading list and then to a seminar setting where reflections were no longer enough. In class she was repeatedly asked to point to the passage that supported a claim, and she learned that her gaps were not only informational but a matter of how she was learning. The discipline taught her to ground opinions in the text, ask better questions, tolerate unresolved ones and understand a position before judging it, with humility tied to learning. She is now continuing with the Graham School's Middle Ages sequence and an introduction to Greek, and she closes with the full two-year reading list.
points: Reading widely on your own builds love of the classics, but serious texts like Plato usually require a community to read well.
Great Books seminars shift the standard from personal reaction to evidence from the text, which exposes how you learn, not just what you lack.
Learning to follow an author's reasoning and state a disagreeing view fairly before judging it is presented as a form of humility.
Leaving questions unresolved is part of the method, since sometimes the question is the point.
Adult liberal education is a lifelong pursuit, shown here by enrolling in a two-year medieval sequence and beginning ancient Greek.
quotes: I prefer the freedom to study whatever interests me. I want to know a variety of things well, like a Renaissance woman.
This list was another level of hard. Some of the literature overlapped with Bauer’s list, but the curriculum included far more philosophy and political theory than I had ever read.
Just like before, I realized that reading Plato was going to require a village. So instead of staring at the list wondering where to begin, I signed up for the Basic Program.
I knew I had a lot of holes in my education. I thought they were just informational holes. But I soon realized how much I still had to learn.
In class, I would make a comment, and my instructors would ask me where I saw that in the text. Frantically, I’d search through the pages as everyone silently looked on.

After a couple of years of experiencing these ups and downs, I learned that my opinions needed to be grounded in the text. I learned to ask better questions and to leave questions unresolved. Sometimes the question was the point.

And regardless of how I felt about it, I needed to be able to follow the author’s reasoning, explain the position I disagreed with, and understand a passage before judging it. Humility went hand in hand with learning.
The Middle Ages course runs for two years. The goal of the course is to understand what shaped medieval thought.
